items.body:
Off Leash update 20 November 2026

MYANMAR
•The International Court of Justice (ICJ) found Myanmar guilty of genocide against Rohingya Muslims in 2017, when it drove around 700,000 Rohingyas from their homes, killing around 10,000 of them in the process.
•Myanmar can’t appeal, but the verdict is mostly symbolic because it will be hard to enforce. This was the first time the ICJ convicted a country – as opposed to a person – on genocide charges, and it’s hard to imprison an entire country at The Hague.
•A more significant consequence of the ICJ’s judgment against Myanmar is that this case is likely to influence the court’s hearing of the genocide case South Africa is bringing against Israel for its actions in Gaza.

MEETINGS
•I didn’t realize that yesterday was the first time the leaders of the U.S., China, and Russia had ever had a trilateral meeting.
•Not that it accomplished much. Analysts say optics overshadowed policy – which some observers attributed to poor, hasty planning.
•All three leaders espoused the virtues of peace, and they signed a fairly toothless “peace declaration” – even though two of them are actively embroiled in wars they started, and the third (Xi) has ordered his military to prepare to invade Taiwan by 2027. 
•They didn’t talk much about those active or looming wars – or about other thorny issues that keep global superpower leaders up at night, so it wasn’t exactly the Yalta 2.0 that some had hoped for. The friendly photos were nice, though.

UKRAINE
•Pres. Putin lashed out after Ukraine destroyed a critical span of the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea.
•It’s understandable that Putin would be angry over Kerch. It isn’t just a normal bridge – like the three Russia destroyed in Kyiv in retaliation. It was built as a symbol that Russia intended to stay in Crimea after illegally annexing it in 2014, and it’s the main supply route for Crimea’s Russian occupiers.
•Putin claimed he WAS feeling open to signing more local, temporary ceasefires – like the one Melania Trump reportedly brokered in Oleshky last month – but he says he’s now ruled that idea out because of Kerch.
•He also vowed a “painful” response…during the press conference after his trilateral with Trump and Xi, where he noted that the three  “have many converging interests when it comes to resolving regional conflicts, including, of course, the conflict in Ukraine.”

YEMEN
•Yemen’s Houthis struck the skyscraper that houses Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund. Nobody was hurt, but the damage to the building will serve as a visible reminder to Riyadh residents that their country is at war – despite the pretense of “business as usual” their leaders are trying to maintain.

BREXIT
•UK and EU leaders met in Brussels today to discuss dismantling some of the trade barriers that have hindered the UK’s economy since a majority of Brits voted to leave the EU in 2016.
•What they agreed on today could add 0.5% to the UK’s economy – which is only a sliver of the 6-8% of GDP that economists estimate Brexit cost the country. Still, it probably is – as Prime Minister Burnham noted – the “single biggest growth measure we could take in this parliament.”

TECH
•Anthropic’s IPO exceeded its target of $83/share to become the largest-ever public listing, with a valuation of nearly $1.3 trillion. That investor optimism was limited to Anthropic, though: other tech stocks continued the slow decline they’ve suffered in recent weeks.

items.summary: Peter St. Onge argues that Democrats took both houses of Congress on November 3 because voters were furious about grocery and gas prices and the Iran war, not because they gave the party a mandate. He says the winners are treating the result as one, and are pushing a public health-insurance option, a reparations commission covering more than slavery, and a 5 percent annual wealth tax on billionaires. Citing a Forbes growth figure, he says billionaire capital grows about 5 percent a year, so that tax would take the whole gain, and that the base would later be pulled down toward homeowners and profitable small businesses. He argues a $25 minimum wage would make jobs that produce less than that illegal, and that with a May 2025 median wage of $24.51 an hour this would cover about half of American jobs, about 72 million, hitting teenagers and new workers while AI is already replacing entry-level work. He also says Khanna wants ICE abolished, that Democratic leaders back mass amnesty, and that the incoming House is preparing investigations of Trump donors, RFK Jr., and a long target list that includes Stephen Miller and Trump's children.
